name: Dimethylaminoethanol (DMAE)

lead: DMAE is an amino alcohol that appears in some skin-care products marketed for firming and improving skin tone. People use it hoping for tighter-looking skin and fewer visible wrinkles.

It is mainly an industrial chemical, and its bitartrate salt is sold as an oral nootropic. No mechanism for skin firming is documented, and animal work cited for it concerns memory. The only registered human study found involving a DMAE skin product tested a multi-ingredient combination.

paras: Used as a topical cream or serum ingredient, usually in a daily face-care routine, or as an oral supplement. Users of firming products typically apply them for weeks before judging results.
The pure industrial liquid is flammable and corrosive and carries hazard warnings. Safety data for cosmetic or supplement use in people are limited.

angle.text: DMAE is an ingredient in skin-firming creams marketed for a tighter, smoother look, and is also sold as an oral nootropic. The only registered human study found tested a multi-ingredient product.

lead: Dimethylaminoethanol (DMAE, also deanol, DMEA) is an ingredient in some skin-care gels and creams sold for firming and smoothing aging skin. People use it topically in the hope of tighter-looking skin, softer fine lines on the forehead and around the eyes, and a fuller lip shape [1]. It is also sold as the bitartrate salt in oral nootropic supplements [2][3].

DMAE is an analog of choline and a precursor of acetylcholine. A 2005 review in the American Journal of Clinical Dermatology proposed that acetylcholine acts as a cytokine-like signal in skin that regulates cell proliferation, differentiation and secretion, which could underlie DMAE's cutaneous activity [1].

Outside cosmetics, DMAE is mainly an industrial chemical used as a curing agent for polyurethanes and epoxy resins and as an intermediate for other compounds [2][3]. In the mid-20th century and 1970s it was also studied as a drug, including in tardive dyskinesia trials [4].
infobox: Bitartrate salt (about 37% DMAE) in supplements; topical cosmetic ingredient [3]

paras: DMAE is a bifunctional molecule carrying a tertiary amine and a primary alcohol. It is prepared industrially by ethoxylation of dimethylamine and is a flammable, corrosive liquid with a fishy odour. [3] Reported oral LD50 in rats is around 1 to 2 g per kg depending on the source. [2][3]

The 2005 review describes DMAE as a choline analog and precursor of acetylcholine. It notes growing evidence that acetylcholine acts as a ubiquitous cytokine-like molecule regulating proliferation, differentiation, movement and secretion of cells in a paracrine and autocrine way, and suggests this modulatory role may contribute to DMAE's skin activity [1].

Cosmetic products use DMAE, often as the bitartrate salt at low percentage concentrations, as a skin-firming ingredient [2]. Manufacturers and proponents describe it as tightening sagging skin and improving tone [3]. The studied form was a 3% facial gel applied daily [1].

DMAE bitartrate is sold as an oral nootropic. Animal studies cited by Wikipedia suggest possible benefit for spatial and working memory, and a pyroglutamate form has been studied against scopolamine-induced memory deficits. [3]

Concentrated DMAE is classified under GHS as corrosive and acutely toxic by several routes, with hazard statements for skin burns and eye damage. This is an industrial-handling classification and does not directly describe finished cosmetic products. [3][2]
DMAE is rarely discussed as a standalone item on appearance forums. On T Nation it appears mainly as an ingredient (deanol bitartrate) in stimulant-style and mood supplements [5][6].

A randomized, placebo-controlled study reviewed in 2005 tested a 3% DMAE facial gel applied daily for 16 weeks. It was reported as safe and efficacious (p < 0.05) for forehead lines and periorbital fine wrinkles and for lip shape, fullness and the overall appearance of aging skin. Effects did not regress during a 2-week stop. Trends (p between 0.05 and 0.1) were seen for coarse wrinkles, under-eye dark circles, nasolabial folds, sagging neck skin and neck firmness, and application was well tolerated [1].

A registered phase 2 study (44 participants, completed 2025) tested a serum and cream combining GABA, DMAE, cysteamine and bakuchiol for skin whitening and anti-aging; because several ingredients were combined, it does not isolate DMAE's effect [7].

Oral deanol was studied in the 1970s and 1980s in tardive dyskinesia, with Cochrane reviews of cholinergic drugs covering it; these concern movement disorders, not skin [4]. One report described mood changes (depression in five, hypomania in three of 38 patients) at high oral doses [8].

lore.intro: Community material on DMAE is mostly about its role in supplements rather than skin firming [5].
